plan.title: React vs Vue: Which Should You Learn First?
plan.description: React and Vue are two of the most popular frontend frameworks, and this video compares them on learning curve, jobs, and ecosystem. You will leave with a clear recommendation based on your situation.

beats.narration: You want to build websites, and everyone tells you something different. Learn React. No, learn Vue. Pick wrong, and you might waste weeks. So how do you actually choose?
Here is the decision. We will compare them on three things: how easy they are to learn, how many jobs they offer, and how big their ecosystems are.
Start with learning. Vue is generally easier to begin with. Its templates look like the HTML you already know, and the official docs walk you down one recommended path.
Vue also uses single-file components. Template, script, and style live together in one dot vue file. Someone who knows HTML, CSS, and JavaScript can be productive in days.
React asks a bit more. JSX mixes markup into JavaScript, which needs a mental shift. Hooks have rules. And you face more choices for routing, state, and data fetching.
One warning. Beginners often build a React app, then need a second page and freeze, because React has no router built in. Vue handles that out of the box.
The good news is that the curves converge. Past the first month, productivity in both frameworks looks similar, and Vue's Composition API and React Hooks now follow similar patterns.

props.text: After the first month, the learning curves converge.

beats.narration: Now the other side: work. React dominates the job market, with about sixty-five percent share in one 2026 comparison. More jobs, more tutorials, more answers online.
React's ecosystem is also larger. That makes it a safe choice for many business apps. Vue's ecosystem is smaller, but more cohesive, with official routing and state management.
Vue wins on enjoyment. Developers rate its satisfaction highly, and one guide scores it five stars for small apps and prototypes. React gets four, strong for startups and scalable products.
So here is the verdict. If your goal is a job soon, learn React. Its demand and resources are the biggest, and a meta-framework like Next.js bundles the missing pieces.

hook_close.hook_text: You want to build websites, and everyone tells you something different. Learn React. No, learn Vue. Pick wrong, and you might waste weeks. So how do you actually choose?
hook_close.close_text: The takeaway: choose React for hiring odds, Vue for an easier start. Pick one today, build something real, and you can always learn the other later.

accuracy.reason: The 65% job share is from a single source and presented as a hard pie chart. "Developers rate its satisfaction highly" and the five-star versus four-star ratings come from a small-business blog and are used as evidence of enjoyment. The claim that beginners "freeze" because React has no router is exaggerated.

coverage.reason: It covers learning curve, jobs and ecosystem and gives a recommendation by situation. Performance, tooling (Vite, devtools) and philosophy are missing, and there is no mention of React Native, Nuxt or regional job reality.

structure.reason: Clear arc: criteria, learning, jobs, verdict, and a self-test. A small flaw is that beat 10 on enjoyment sits awkwardly in the jobs and ecosystem section.

hook_ending.reason: The hook of "Learn React. No, learn Vue." creates mild tension. The ending takeaway is fine but is mostly a summary line.

tone.reason: Friendly, beginner-appropriate and non-tribal, with a fair "neither choice is wrong" stance.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well: pie, table, versus, diagram and checklists. The pie is a trivial two-slice chart. Beat 10's gallery of generic coder images does not match the star-rating narration.

originality.reason: Largely follows the sources. The "freeze at a second page" router point is concrete, but most of the rest is generic comparison.

instructions.reason: English, about the right length, with a recommendation by situation. Fewer criteria than the note suggests.

language.reason: Fluent and clear. "Here is the decision" is a slightly odd opener for beat 2, and "dot vue file" is spoken naturally.

defects.quote: React dominates the job market, with about sixty-five percent share in one 2026 comparison.
defects.issue: A single unverified secondary-source figure is turned into a precise pie chart, and the metric (job postings versus usage) is unclear.

defects.quote: Developers rate its satisfaction highly, and one guide scores it five stars for small apps and prototypes.
defects.issue: The star ratings are a business-oriented blog's opinion, not evidence of developer enjoyment. The claim is weak.

defects.quote: then need a second page and freeze, because React has no router built in.
defects.issue: This overstates a blog's warning. The same notes say a meta-framework like Next.js solves it.

defects.quote: We will compare them on three things: how easy they are to learn, how many jobs they offer, and how big their ecosystems are.
defects.issue: Performance, tooling and philosophy are skipped, and the notes had bundle-size data to use.
A fourth criterion appears after the three announced, and it breaks the promised structure.
Generic stock images do not illustrate the claim about ratings and satisfaction.

defects.quote: Pick wrong, and you might waste weeks.
defects.issue: The stakes are small and the framing is generic. This weakens the curiosity of the hook.

defects.quote: If you are new, want fast progress, or just want to enjoy building, pick Vue.
defects.issue: The advice never tells the US viewer that React dominates local hiring, or that Vue jobs are fewer. It also omits the fact that Vue-first learners can still face React-heavy job listings.

missing: Philosophy: library vs framework, JSX vs templates
Caveat that job-share stats vary by region and source
wrong_facts: The 65% React job share comes from a single secondary source and is not verified.
The star ratings are a small-business blog's opinion, not a developer-satisfaction measure.
judge.summary: A clean, fair, well-structured beginner comparison that leans on a few thin blog statistics and omits performance, tooling and philosophy. The hook and ending are serviceable but not memorable.
